title: The Story of the Western Wing
subtitle: May All Lovers in the World Be United
description: "The Story of the Western Wing," full title "Cui Yingying Waits for the Moon in the Western Wing," is a Yuan dynasty drama by Wang Shifu, hailed as "the finest play under heaven." It tells the story of scholar Zhang Gong and the prime minister's daughter Cui Yingying, who meet and fall in love at Pujiu Temple, breaking free from the constraints of feudal propriety to be united. The play spans five acts and twenty-one scenes, with florid language and lingering emotion, standing as the pinnacle of classical Chinese drama.

route.title: The Story of the Western Wing: May All Lovers Be United
route.intro:
Jade-green clouds spread across the sky, / Yellow petals carpet the ground. / The west wind blows sharp and high, / Wild geese fly southward, northward bound. / At dawn, who makes the frosted woods so red? / The parting tears of lovers, it is said.
Wang Shifu, a native of Dadu (present-day Beijing) in the Yuan dynasty, left few biographical traces—yet with one play, "The Story of the Western Wing," he captured the most stirring lovesickness and devotion between men and women. The tale began with Yuan Zhen's "The Story of Yingying" from the Tang dynasty, was expanded by Dong Jieyuan's "The Western Wing in All Keys and Modes" during the Jin dynasty, and was transformed into an immortal masterpiece by Wang Shifu—rising from a tragedy of "seduction and abandonment" to the eternal blessing "May all lovers in the world be united." Let us enter Pujiu Temple in Yongji, Shanxi, and amid the echoes of its millenary pagoda, seek out that legendary love story quietly blooming deep within a pear-flower courtyard.

stops.title: Stop One: Meeting at Pujiu Temple
stops.content: During the Zhenyuan reign of the Tang dynasty, a young scholar named Zhang Gong from Luoyang set out for the capital to take the imperial examinations. Passing through Hezhong Prefecture, he paused before an ancient temple. Shaded by pines and cypresses, its halls rising majestically, this was the renowned Pujiu Temple—the site of what is today the Pujiu Temple Pagoda. Zhang intended only a brief visit, but as he turned a corridor corner deep among flowering shades, he glimpsed a young woman—"Her waist so supple, her grace beyond compare, a thousand charms, ten thousand tender airs, like a willow swaying in the evening breeze." In that single glance, his life was decided. That woman was Cui Yingying, the daughter of the late Prime Minister Cui, who accompanied her mother with the coffin to their ancestral home, lodging temporarily in the western wing of the temple. Zhang fell in love at first sight and resolved immediately: he would not go to the capital, he would renounce all worldly ambition, and he would stay in this temple. He rented a monk's cell from the abbot, which happened to share a wall with the western wing. The seed of love quietly sprouted amid the evening drums and morning bells of this millenary temple. Pujiu Temple lies in Yongji, southern Shanxi—a land of mountain and river splendor. Not far to the west stands the Xiezhou Guandi Temple, known as the "ancestor of martial temples," the hometown of Lord Guan, sacred ground of eternal loyalty. A short way south, in Ruicheng's Yongle Town, the Yongle Palace astounds the world with its murals—the "Chart of the Celestial Court" from the Yuan dynasty, where 290 heavenly beings, their robes flowing, stand in majestic vigor, as if watching human joys and sorrows from the clouds. The love story that unfolded in this land was destined to be extraordinary.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Pear-Flower Courtyard Reflects the Western Wing
stops.content: After Zhang settled in the temple, he longed daily to catch a glimpse of Yingying. At last, his chance came—the Cui family held a requiem service in the western wing for the late prime minister, and Zhang managed to sneak into the ceremony, burning incense as he prayed. Under the hazy moonlight, he and Yingying gazed at each other across the flowers—he was "dazzled and speechless, his soul soaring to the skies," while she was "the scent of orchids still lingering, the sound of jade ornaments fading away." In that courtyard, pear blossoms fell like snow, scattered by the spring breeze. But the path of love was never smooth. The rebel general Sun Feihu surrounded Pujiu Temple, demanding Yingying be handed over. In desperation, Madam Cui promised publicly, "Whoever can drive away the bandits shall have my daughter as his wife." Zhang sent a letter summoning the White Horse General, who lifted the siege. Yet Madam Cui reneged on her promise, insisting the two treat each other only as "brother and sister." From then on came the barriers of high walls and deep courtyards, the matchmaking of the maid Hongniang, the danger of climbing the wall for secret rendezvous, and the agony of separation and longing—every brick, every blade of grass at Pujiu Temple bore witness to this breathtaking romance. The whitewashed wall separating the eastern and western wings became the most famous wall in Chinese literary history. Zhang played his zither on one side, while Yingying listened from the other—"His thoughts are endless, my understanding runs deep; a pair of young phoenixes, parted, cannot sleep." A thousand years later, standing beneath the Pujiu Temple Pagoda and listening intently, you can almost still hear that plaintive yet persistent zither music. And wonderfully, if you strike a stone before the pagoda, it echoes like the croaking of frogs—as if the very earth were answering that eternal sigh.

stops.title: Stop Three: Farewell at the Long Pavilion
stops.content: Madam Cui could not bear to entrust her daughter to a penniless scholar. She forced Zhang to go to the capital for the examinations—"If you earn an official rank, come see me. If you fail, do not return!" With that command, one of the most immortal farewell scenes in all literature was born. By the banks of the Yellow River, at a十里-long pavilion. The autumn wind had risen, yellow leaves carpeted the ancient road, and the sky was a blue so intense it seemed about to shatter. In Yingying's eyes, the autumn colors were desolate—not because autumn itself is bleak, but because her heart had shattered into these fallen leaves. "Jade-green clouds spread across the sky, / Yellow petals carpet the ground. / The west wind blows sharp and high, / Wild geese fly southward, northward bound. / At dawn, who makes the frosted woods so red? / The parting tears of lovers, it is said." This lyric [Duan Zhenghao] is renowned as among the most beautiful in all Yuan opera: jade sky, white clouds, a carpet of yellow petals swaying in the west wind, wild geese flying south in a "V"—every stroke a pure description of scenery, yet when the final line "The parting tears of lovers, it is said" arrives, all that beauty transforms into the deepest sorrow of separation. Wang Shifu does not write of Yingying weeping; he lets heaven and earth weep on her behalf—the red of the frosted woods is dyed by parting tears, the yellow petals strewn across the ground are scattered from a broken heart. Yingying did not worry whether Zhang would pass the examinations. Her fear was far more intimate—"Don't you worry about talent failing to bring fortune; I only fear you'll take another wife and abandon me." The Cui Yingying Wang Shifu created is not at all the passive, obedient aristocratic lady of traditional literature. She dares to love, dares to hate, dares to speak, dares to act—she is the first woman in Chinese drama to fight for her own destiny. She wants no titled nobility, no phoenix coronet—she only wants the man who played the zither for her beneath the western wing's moonlight. "Just to be a pair of lotus flowers on one stem is better than being the top scholar." Before parting, she repeats over and over, "In desolate villages where rain and dew fall, rest early; at rustic inns where wind and frost bite, rise late." The simplest words hide the deepest love—rank and riches can all be abandoned, only your safe return matters. When one person cares so much for another's comfort in such detail, that is the deepest love in all the world. The Long Pavilion, the ancient road, the setting sun—one man, one horse, receding into the distance. Yingying stood alone in the autumn wind, her robes fluttering, her tears blurring the departing figure. Behind her, the Yellow River, laden with silt, glowed dark-golden in the sunset and flowed eastward with a heavy burden—as if the earth itself were sighing for her. This land east of the river has been steeped in loyalty since ancient times. South of the Long Pavilion, in Ruicheng's Yongle Town, the Yongle Palace, hailed as the "Oriental Art Gallery," has stood silently for over seven hundred years—its Yuan-dynasty "Chart of the Celestial Court" stretching across 400 square meters with 290 celestial beings. Immortals never age while the mortal world undergoes endless change, yet the flowing robes in the mural seem to echo that corner of Yingying's skirt blown by the west wind at the Long Pavilion. Further west to Xiezhou, the Xiezhou Guandi Temple embodies a loyalty that has spanned a millennium—Lord Guan's story of honoring his pledge with his life, of guarding loyalty to the end, resonates deeply with Yingying's words, "Just to be a pair of lotus flowers on one stem is better than being the top scholar." The people of this land have always known that some things matter more than worldly glory.

stops.title: Stop Four: Journey to Chang'an for the Examinations
stops.content: Zhang Gong traveled through wind and dust to reach Chang'an. The Tang-dynasty civil examinations were held in the Department of State Affairs, and scholars from across the empire gathered in the capital. He studied through the night in his lodgings, yet his thoughts were never entirely on the classics and policy essays—Yingying's shadow always flickered before his lamp. Whenever his mind wandered from his books, he could almost hear her softly reminding him, "In desolate villages where rain and dew fall, rest early; at rustic inns where wind and frost bite, rise late." He would steady himself and bury his head in his studies again. Day after day, by the green lamp and yellowed scrolls, amidst the fierce competition of thousands, a promise made at Pujiu Temple in Yongji, Shanxi, weighed heavier than any official rank. During those days, he also wandered through Chang'an's streets. The Tang capital possessed an unrivaled grandeur—its 108 wards arranged like a chessboard, the Vermilion Bird Avenue over a hundred meters wide, the Eastern and Western Markets gathering rare goods from across the world. Yet all this splendor, in his eyes, could not compare to that small courtyard in the western wing of Pujiu Temple. One dusk, he climbed the city wall and gazed westward—the setting sun like molten gold, the ten thousand lamps of Chang'an lighting up one by one, but in his heart there was only that single lamp burning for him east of the river. At last, the examination day arrived. Zhang entered the hall, unrolled his paper, and his literary inspiration flowed like a spring. Perhaps it was because he had played so much zither and written so many poems in the moonlit nights at Pujiu Temple—ten years of study, plus this unforgettable love, gave his essays a depth of feeling unmatched by any other candidate. After several rounds, he passed with highest honors. The news reached Pujiu Temple, and Yingying wept for joy—not because she would become the wife of a top scholar, but because her Zhang Gong could finally come home. However, the Ministry of Appointments' selection process was long and tedious; he waited in the capital for months. The pain of longing was even more torturous than the unfulfilled love before the examinations—this was the longest night before dawn. He wrote letters to Yingying without cease, every one densely filled, urging her to take care, telling her that his return was near. Today, the relics of Tang-dynasty Chang'an can still be touched in Xi'an. The road Zhang traveled—from Yongji east of the river, westward through the Tong Pass, across the Guanzhong Plain, to Chang'an—you can still walk this path today. Enter the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, a seven-story square pagoda designed and built by Xuanzang himself, the sacred site where successful candidates in the Tang dynasty inscribed their names—the "Pagoda Inscription." Countless newly minted scholars proudly carved their names beneath this pagoda, and Zhang Gong was probably among them. Ascend to the top and gaze into the distance—the eight hundred li of the Qinchuan Plain spread out before you. What you see is the same vast landscape that Zhang Gong saw while waiting for his appointment thirteen centuries ago. Walk along the Xi'an City Wall—built in the Ming dynasty on the foundations of the Tang Chang'an city, it measures 13.7 kilometers in circumference and is the best-preserved ancient city wall in the world. Stand on the wall and look eastward—across the Ba River, across the Wei River, across the Tong Pass—there lies the land east of the river, there lies Pujiu Temple, there lies the woman who has been waiting for months beneath the pear tree. With rank secured and heart racing homeward, Zhang finally understood the truth of Yingying's words: "Just to be a pair of lotus flowers on one stem is better than being the top scholar."

stops.title: Stop Five: Finally United
stops.content: "Eternal, with no parting, / Forever united without end. / May all lovers in the world be united." At last, Zhang Gong returned home in honor. At the十里-long pavilion, spring breezes greeted him—no more autumn winds and yellow leaves, no more tears of parting. Madam Cui no longer objected—a newly minted top scholar was a status sufficient to overcome her prejudice against the match. Pujiu Temple was festooned with lanterns and colored silk. The pear blossoms in the western wing bloomed again, each petal white as snow, as if heaven and earth themselves were showering blessings upon the reunited lovers. From the prototype tragedy of "seduction and abandonment" in Yuan Zhen's Tang-dynasty story, to the first reversal in Dong Jieyuan's Jin-dynasty adaptation, to Wang Shifu's heartwarming conclusion of "May all lovers in the world be united"—the evolution of "The Story of the Western Wing" mirrors the great journey of the Chinese conception of love from repression to liberation. This Pujiu Temple Pagoda—also known as the Yingying Pagoda—has borne witness to the prayers of countless lovelorn souls over the centuries. Strike a stone and listen to the frog-like echo—it sounds like the zither music that drifted across the wall on that spring night, distant, persistent, never fading. Today, when you come to Yongji, visit the Yongle Palace and its Yuan-dynasty murals of the celestial realm, pay homage at the Xiezhou Guandi Temple where loyalty echoes through millennia, then return to the ancient and solemn Pujiu Temple. Stand for a while beneath the pear tree in the western wing. You will understand: the truly great drama is not performed on a stage, but in every person's life.

stops.title: Stop Six: Looking Back from Chang'an: Love Beyond Time
stops.content: After Zhang Gong passed the examinations with highest honors, he waited in Chang'an for the Ministry of Appointments to assign him a post. During those days, he walked the streets and alleys of Chang'an, taking in the majestic sights of the imperial capital—the imposing Hanyuan Hall of the Daming Palace, the rippling blue waters of the Taiye Pool, the bustling Eastern and Western Markets crowded with merchants from all directions. Yet all this splendor, in his eyes, could not compare to that small courtyard in the western wing of Pujiu Temple. He wrote to Yingying of his lovesickness: "This short paper cannot contain the depth of my longing, these few words cannot express the fullness of my heart." Today, when you come to Xi'an, step into the Daming Palace Ruins, stand on the rammed-earth platform of Hanyuan Hall and gaze westward—thirteen centuries ago, Zhang Gong galloped along this ancient road beside the Wei River, racing eastward toward the land of Hedong, toward the woman waiting for him beneath the pear tree. The ruins of Daming Palace have witnessed countless partings and reunions—of emperors, of poets, of generals—and the parting of Zhang and Yingying was merely one among the ten thousand stories of Chang'an. Yet it is precisely this story that, after a thousand years, still makes everyone who reads "Jade-green clouds spread across the sky" feel their heart stir. Wang Shifu did not write what happened after Zhang Gong returned to Pujiu Temple—he stopped at the most beautiful moment: "Eternal, with no parting, forever united without end." Chinese classical literature is not lacking in well-matched, perfect marriages, but "The Story of the Western Wing" bequeathed to posterity not a wedding, but a belief—a belief that love can transcend social standing, that persistence can overcome convention, that "May all lovers in the world be united" is not an empty phrase. Though the Daming Palace has long since become ruins, those words about courage and devotion will never become rubble. Like the city walls of Chang'an, they have stood for a thousand years through wind and rain, and will continue to stand forever.
